claims.text: An equal-parts Fe-Co-Ni-Mn-Cu coating can be deposited homogeneously on an SS-304 substrate.
The Fe-Co-Ni-Mn-Cu system can form a (Fe,Co,Ni,Mn,Cu)3O4 high-entropy spinel during oxidation in air.
The high-entropy spinel oxide is protective.
The protective spinel forms rapidly in an oxidizing tribocorrosion environment.
Overall tribocorrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is governed by the dynamic interplay between mechanical wear and a self-healing oxide film.
Sliding mechanically removes or ruptures the protective oxide film and exposes fresh alloy.
In the presence of oxygen, exposed alloy rapidly re-oxidizes and re-establishes the protective film.
The rate of oxide regeneration relative to its rate of mechanical removal determines the wear-corrosion balance.
Changing sliding load or speed changes the degree of oxide-film rupture.
Matched static-corrosion and inert-medium pure-wear tests can isolate corrosion and wear contributions from the simultaneous tribocorrosion response.
Moderate sliding loads establish a dynamic equilibrium between film removal and regeneration.
At moderate loads, net degradation is lower than the sum expected if wear and corrosion acted independently.
At sufficiently high loads, oxide-film rupture outpaces regeneration.
When film rupture outpaces regeneration, both wear and corrosion contributions increase relative to the baseline.
Compositions favoring rapid oxide formation show the greatest improvement relative to static-corrosion or isolated-wear conditions.
The proposed behavior requires sufficient oxygen and elements capable of forming a robust protective spinel.
The proposed mechanism should fail in oxygen-depleted conditions or in alloys unable to form a robust protective oxide.
